\chapter{If, and When}
\label{ch:gu-if-and-when}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can suppose something with a two-part condition and place one event against another in time.}

The first joining words that open their clause rather than following it. Gujarati marks BOTH ends of a condition -- jo ... to ... -- where English marks only the first, and the writing lesson carries the warning that jo hides inside aavjo and jovun, which is why the inventory found sixteen apparent hits and no real ones.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[jo]{\gu{જો} (jo) — if}

\label{lesson:GU-C35-jo}



\begin{quote}
One chapter back, the word that draws a conclusion. Three chapters back, at the end of its chapter, the word that means both \emph{but} and \emph{also}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{tethī}, then \emph{paṇ}
\end{itemize}

Every joining word so far has taken two things that are \textbf{true} and put them together. This one takes something that \textbf{might not be}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જો}} \emph{(something that might be so)} …
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{જો}} stands at the \textbf{front} of the condition, where English also puts \emph{if}. That is unusual for this book: most of the small words you have met — \textbf{\gu{માટે}}, \textbf{\gu{પણ}} in its \emph{also} sense, the postpositions — come \textbf{after} what they apply to. \textbf{\gu{જો}} comes first, and that alone tells your ear a condition is starting.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jo}, then any sentence you can already say.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the sentence flat, then the same sentence with \emph{jo} in front.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jo} and \emph{māṭe} back to back — one leads, one follows.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\gu{જો}} stand, and why is that worth noticing? (At the front — most small words in this book come after what they apply to.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jo … to …]{\gu{જો} … \gu{તો} … (jo … to …) — if … then …}

\label{lesson:GU-C35-jo-to}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back: the word that opens a condition. Four chapters back, at the head of the repair chapter: the negator.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{jo}, and \emph{nathī}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Gujarati usually marks \textbf{both} ends of a condition:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જો}} \emph{(condition)}, \textbf{\gu{તો}} \emph{(result)}
\end{quote}

English says \emph{if it is late, I will go} and marks only the front. Gujarati puts \textbf{\gu{તો}} at the head of the result as well, so the sentence announces its two halves. Beginners often leave \textbf{\gu{તો}} out; it is understood, but the full pair is what you will hear.

\textbf{\gu{તો}} is a worn-down demonstrative — the sentence says, in effect, \emph{if … that …} — which is why it sits at the head of the result rather than inside it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{jo} + a condition, \emph{to} + a result.
  \item \emph{Build:} the same, with the result negative.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the pair with \emph{to}, then without it. Both are grammatical.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Make a two-part condition. Which half does English leave unmarked that Gujarati marks? (The result — \emph{to}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jo]{\gu{જો} reaches the page}

\label{lesson:GU-C35-jo-write}



\begin{quote}
Three chapters back you wrote the joining word. Write \textbf{\gu{અને}} once from memory before anything is uncovered.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — two signs, and a caution}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જ}} — \emph{ja} · \textbf{\gu{ો}} — the \emph{o} stroke
\end{quote}

Both old. But \textbf{\gu{જો}} is worth extra care for a reason the other words in this run did not have: \textbf{the same two letters appear inside words you already know that have nothing to do with \emph{if}}. They turn up at the end of the farewell \textbf{\gu{આવજો}}, and at the start of the verb \textbf{\gu{જોવું}}, \emph{to see}.

So when you meet \textbf{\gu{જો}} on a page, check that it is standing \textbf{alone} and at the \textbf{front} of its clause. Inside a longer word it is not this word at all.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Copy \textbf{\gu{જો}} once with the model in view. Then write it again with a space after it, at the front of a line, which is where it belongs.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you tell the \emph{if} \textbf{\gu{જો}} from the same two signs inside a longer word? (It stands alone, at the front of its clause.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jyāre]{\gu{જ્યારે} (jyāre) — when}

\label{lesson:GU-C35-jyaare}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back you wrote \textbf{\gu{જો}}. One chapter back, the word that answers \emph{why}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\gu{જો}}, and \emph{kemke}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જ્યારે}} \emph{(one event)}, \emph{(the other)}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{જ્યારે}} sets two events against each other in time — \emph{when this, that}. Like \textbf{\gu{જો}}, it opens its clause rather than following it.

It is not a random shape. The \textbf{\gu{જ્}-} at its front belongs to a large family: Gujarati builds a whole set of clause-openers on that one stem, and you are learning a single member of it here rather than the pattern all at once.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{jyāre} + an event, then a second event.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{jo} and \emph{jyāre} on the same two clauses — one supposes, one times.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jyāre} slowly; the \textbf{\gu{જ્યા}-} is one sound, not two.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say a \emph{when} sentence. What is the difference between opening with \textbf{\gu{જો}} and opening with \textbf{\gu{જ્યારે}}? (\emph{jo} supposes something might be so; \emph{jyāre} places it in time.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Conditions and times, all together}

\label{lesson:GU-C35-condition-checkpoint}



\begin{quote}
No new words. One run through the two clause-openers this chapter added, against the ones behind them.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{જો}} — \emph{if}, standing at the front of its clause.
  \item \textbf{\gu{જો} … \gu{તો} …} — both ends marked, which is what you will hear.
  \item \textbf{\gu{જો}} on the page, and how to tell it from the same signs inside \textbf{\gu{આવજો}}.
  \item \textbf{\gu{જ્યારે}} — \emph{when}, placing one event against another.
\end{itemize}

Five chapters ago this book could not join two sentences at all. It can now suppose one, time one against another, give a reason for one, and set two against each other.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} one \emph{jo … to …} sentence.
  \item \emph{Build:} one \emph{jyāre} sentence.
  \item \emph{Build:} one \emph{kemke} answer, from the chapter before.
  \item \emph{Say it:} two things joined by \emph{ane}, from three chapters back.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Suppose something, then time something. Next chapter: \textbf{he}, \textbf{she}, \textbf{we}, and the word that lets you say \emph{the one who}.
